learnMode.summary: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the family and the measures from its own numbers, shows the question, then reveals the colour coding, the checklist and the answer together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A relation that holds at one point of the sweep is a position, not a property of the family. Breaks: A property judged from the drawn case, so a parallelogram in a rectangle position is credited with right angles. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): Reaching a special position does not add a property to the family that was swept. Breaks: Reading a coincidence at one parameter value as a new guaranteed property. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): Equal and supplementary are different relations that coincide only at 90 degrees. Breaks: Equality assumed where supplementarity holds, so adjacent angles in a parallelogram are expected to be equal. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): A mark is a claim the family forces, so an unmarked pair is a pair nothing guarantees. Breaks: Expecting every quadrilateral to carry the parallelogram marks, so a trapezium is read as one. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): A proposed property set is refuted by one figure that satisfies it and sits outside the family. Breaks: Believing a set of properties that every member has is automatically enough to define the family.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens on a parallelogram with the checklist HIDDEN and asks whether next door angles will add to 180 or be equal. Beat 2 sweeps the shape parameter while the equal sides hold their matching colours and the linking arcs on adjacent angles stay at 180. Beat 3 switches preset to a rectangle, where the same arcs now also read 90 each, so what the family adds is visible as a change in the marks. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setFamily, sweep, revealRow and say. No drag: the agent sets the parameter by value, never by sweeping continuously.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the parallelogram with the equal sides coloured, no arcs drawn and the checklist hidden, and ask the class to say out loud whether next door angles add to 180 or are equal. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Target family parallelogram at the opening parameter. Never draw an arc or reveal a checklist row before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Sweep the shape parameter slowly from one end of its range to the other and point at the linking arc as it holds while the angles themselves keep changing. Target family parallelogram, a sweep across the full parameter range. Read the two angle values and the linking arc total from the tool's own readouts, never from this plan. Call 3. Change the family preset to rectangle with the same arcs still drawn, and ask the class what the extra condition bought. Target family rectangle. Say what the equal pair and the supplementary pair each now read, taking both numbers from the tool's own state.

hunts: NEVER FLICKERS: sweep a parallelogram from end to end and list every mark that never goes out.
POSITION HUNT: find the parameter value where a rhombus shows right angles, then sweep past it.
TOO WEAK: propose a property set, look at the figure the tool draws, and say what is missing.
FAMILY LADDER: switch from parallelogram to rectangle to square and name what each step bought.

observationsAndConclusions.why: Each of them is 180 minus the same adjacent angle, so the two can never come apart
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Through the whole sweep the two opposite angle readouts stay equal to each other
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Opposite angles equal is forced by the parallelogram and not by the position it happens to be in

observationsAndConclusions.why: That pair lies between the same two parallel sides, so the two angles must together make a straight angle
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The linking arc on a next door pair reads 180 at every value of the sweep
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Adjacent angles are supplementary and not equal, which is exactly the pair students swap

observationsAndConclusions.why: Ninety and ninety are equal to each other and also add to 180, so the two relations agree at that one value
observationsAndConclusions.observe: At the rectangle preset the equal pair and the supplementary pair give the same number
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Agreement in one family is not sameness, which is why a rectangle is the worst figure to learn the difference from

media.description: One lettered quadrilateral stands on a plain ground with a property checklist beside it. Equal sides carry matching hatch ticks and a shared colour, equal angles carry same-radius arcs, the parallel pairs carry arrowhead chevrons, and every angle pair the family forces to add to 180 is joined by a linking arc that prints the SUM rather than the word supplementary. A shape parameter sweeps the figure inside its family, and the marks the family forces never flicker while a relation that merely happens to hold at one value is drawn dashed and captioned 'at this value only' — so a coincidence can be watched switching off. Switching the family preset from parallelogram to rectangle, rhombus or square ADDS one condition at a time and the checklist grows without ever resetting, which is how the inclusive classification is read off the list rather than off the outline. Free Play lets the student predict each checklist row before opening it and then test a proposed minimum property set, which the tool answers by drawing a figure that satisfies the set and sits outside the family. Practice serves a session drawn from a thirty item pool on a difficulty ladder, each item rendering the figure its own question describes, with the asked measure masked until the answer is in.

mods.ai_demo: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens on a parallelogram with the checklist HIDDEN and asks whether next door angles will add to 180 or be equal. Beat 2 sweeps the shape parameter while the equal sides hold their matching colours and the linking arcs on adjacent angles stay at 180. Beat 3 switches preset to a rectangle, where the same arcs now also read 90 each, so what the family adds is visible as a change in the marks. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setFamily, sweep, revealRow and say. No drag: the agent sets the parameter by value, never by sweeping continuously.

concept.notation: Equal sides are drawn in matching colours, equal angles carry matching arcs, and a supplementary pair is joined by a single linking arc labelled 180.
concept.statement: Each family fixes a particular pattern of equal and supplementary relations. In a parallelogram opposite sides are equal, opposite angles are equal and adjacent angles are supplementary. Adding one more condition moves you to a rectangle or a rhombus, and adding both gives a square, so the families differ by which relations they force and not by how they happen to look.
prerequisites: the angle sum of a quadrilateral
misconceptions: Opposite angles confused with adjacent ones, so the pair that is equal and the pair that is supplementary are swapped.
Equality assumed where supplementarity holds, so adjacent angles in a parallelogram are expected to be equal.
concept.why_it_is_true: In a parallelogram a pair of adjacent angles sits between the same two parallel sides, so they are co-interior and add to 180. The opposite angles are then each 180 minus the same value, so they are equal to each other. The colour coding and the linking arcs make those two different relations visually different, which is exactly where the confusion lives.
worked_numbers: In a parallelogram with one angle of 70, the adjacent angle is 110 and the opposite angle is 70 again.
In a rectangle every one of those values is 90, so equal and supplementary agree by coincidence.
In a rhombus of side 6 all four sides share one colour, while the angles still split into two equal pairs.

extra: A sliding gate whose slanted bars keep their next door angles adding to a straight angle
A folding ironing board whose opposite legs keep the same angle as it opens
A window blind whose slats stay parallel at every setting
A bicycle stand leaning over, with its opposite bars still equal
A hand held paper fan whose ribs keep two matching angles
A book held open at a slant, so the page corners are no longer square
A diamond shaped road sign with four equal sides and not one right angle
A carrom board and a chess board, both with four equal sides and four right angles
A wall tile pattern where every slanted tile shares the same pair of angles
textbook: Constructing a quadrilateral with two pairs of parallel sides that do not meet at right angles
Finding the remaining angles of a parallelogram when one of them is given
Finding the remaining angles of a trapezium from the angle already marked
Asking whether squares are the only quadrilaterals with all four sides equal
Finding all the sides and angles of the figure made by joining two equilateral triangles
Deciding what kind of quadrilateral has its opposite sides equal, using a diagonal and congruent triangles

answer_key.worked: In a parallelogram opposite angles are equal and adjacent angles add to 180, and the same two relations survive the whole sweep.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn figure: the missing side or angle in the named family, or which pairs the marks currently join.
answer_key.precision: Presets are defined by construction rules rather than fixed coordinates, so every measure is derived and the family cannot be left by sweeping. Equality uses a tolerance of 0.5 degrees and 0.01 units.
answer_key.ground_truth: measures(family, parameter) = the sides, angles and diagonals produced by the construction. equalPairs(measures) and supplementaryPairs(measures) = the pairs the marks join, evaluated live. minimalSet(family) = the smallest condition set whose figures are exactly that family.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.case: A parallelogram swept into a rectangle position
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The extra equalities light and the tool says they are true at this parameter value but not part of the family. Sweeping on turns them off again.

edge_cases.case: A rhombus swept into a square position
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Every side keeps one colour and the angles all reach 90 at once. The tool names the position rather than the family, so the coincidence is not mistaken for a property.

edge_cases.case: A trapezium with only one pair of parallel sides
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Only the co-interior pairs on the legs carry linking arcs. The tool never marks a relation that the family does not force.

edge_cases.case: A proposed minimal set that is too weak
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The tool generates a figure that satisfies the set but is outside the family and asks whether it belongs, so the set is tested rather than marked.

edge_cases.case: The end of a parameter sweep
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The sweep stops before the figure degenerates, with the reason on screen, because a flattened figure has no angles to mark.

steps: The parallelogram construction forces 3 relations: the opposite sides are equal; the opposite angles are equal; next door angles add to 180.
Equal angles all round is not one of them.
This is one value of the sweep, where the figure sits in a rectangle position.
Sweeping on turns both of the new marks off again.
So they name a position and not a property of the family.
items.answer: No: they hold at this parameter value only, and sweeping on turns them off
items.method: Separate a relation that holds at one parameter value from one the family forces

steps: A rhombus forces 4 relations, including all four sides equal.
All four angles equal is not among them.
At this parameter value the angles happen to arrive at 90 together.
Sweeping on moves them apart again while the side colours stay put.
So the tool names the position and leaves the family list alone.
items.answer: The position: the sides stay equal for the family, and the right angles belong to this value of the sweep
items.method: Decide what a rhombus in a square position has gained

steps: Next door angles in any parallelogram add to 180.
In a rectangle each of them measures 90.
180 minus 90 is 90, so the supplement of one is the other.
The two relations agree here because 90 is its own supplement.
Sweep to a parallelogram with an angle of 70 and one reads 70 while the other reads 110.
items.answer: No: they agree only because 90 is its own supplement, and they part company as soon as the angle moves
items.method: Distinguish equal from supplementary where the two happen to agree
items.question: In a rectangle two next door angles are both equal and add to 180. Does that make equal and supplementary the same relation?

stickers.type_method: Distinguish equal from supplementary where the two happen to agree

items.checkpoint: Equal and supplementary are different relations that coincide only at 90 degrees.
items.misconception: Equality assumed where supplementarity holds, so adjacent angles in a parallelogram are expected to be equal.

steps: A linking arc marks a pair the family forces to add to 180.
Only the two legs run between the single pair of parallel sides.
So only the angle pairs on those legs are co-interior.
The remaining pairs are not forced by anything, so marking them would claim a property the family does not give.
The trapezium therefore forces 0 of the listed relations.
items.answer: Only the pairs on the two legs, because a mark the family cannot guarantee would be a false claim
items.method: Predict which marks a trapezium carries
items.question: A trapezium with only one pair of parallel sides is loaded. Which angle pairs carry a linking arc, and why not the others?

stickers.type_method: Predict which marks a trapezium carries

items.checkpoint: A mark is a claim the family forces, so an unmarked pair is a pair nothing guarantees.
items.misconception: Expecting every quadrilateral to carry the parallelogram marks, so a trapezium is read as one.

steps: The proposed set is a claim that nothing outside the family can satisfy it.
The tool builds a figure that satisfies the set.
That figure has one pair of equal sides and no parallel pair at all.
It is outside the family, so the proposed set is too weak.
A set is minimum only when nothing outside the family can meet it.
items.answer: That the set is too weak, because a figure outside the family satisfies it
items.method: Test a proposed minimum property set against a figure outside the family

teaching_notes: Beat 1 states the two relations side by side on one figure, because the misconception is that there is only one. The linking arc prints 70° + 110° = 180° while the two opposite arcs both read 70°: the class can see that the pair that is EQUAL and the pair that ADDS TO 180 are different pairs, and that they are marked with different devices for exactly that reason.

Beat 2 is the justification, and it needs motion. The figure is swept from one end of its range to the other; every number on screen changes and the same two marks hold throughout, because a pair of next-door angles sits between the same two parallel sides and is therefore co-interior. What survives the sweep is what the family guarantees — that is the whole argument and it cannot be made from a still frame.

Beat 3 adds one condition. The preset moves to a rectangle and the checklist GROWS: the three parallelogram rows stay ticked and a fourth lights. That is the inclusive hierarchy read off the list, and it is also where equal and supplementary agree — each next-door angle reads 90 and 90 is its own supplement — which is precisely why a rectangle is the worst figure to learn the difference from.

media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Use the parallel sides of a parallelogram to determine its angles, sides and diagonals. Key teaching points: 1) Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal. 2) Neighbouring angles add to a straight angle. 3) Opposite sides are equal in length. 4) The diagonals cut each other exactly in half. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often assume all four angles of a parallelogram are equal. 2) Students often think the diagonals of a parallelogram are equal. Pause points: 0:25, at the end of a hidden pattern: ask what the angle opposite a given one must be. 0:25, just before the open question: ask what happens where the diagonals cross. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask why the parallel sides lock the angles. After viewing, ask whether the diagonals are equal.

content.text: A parallelogram is a quadrilateral whose opposite sides are parallel. In any parallelogram, the opposite angles are equal, and each pair of adjacent angles (two angles sharing a side) adds up to 180 degrees. The reason is that a side acts as a transversal crossing the two parallel sides, and the two angles on the same side of it are co-interior angles, which are always supplementary. From this, if you know one angle you know them all: the opposite angle repeats it, and each neighbouring angle is its supplement. So the four angles read as a value, its supplement, the value again, and the supplement again, going around. When every angle is 90 degrees the parallelogram is a rectangle.

content.text: In a parallelogram the opposite sides are equal, so its perimeter is twice the sum of two adjacent sides. Its two diagonals always bisect each other, meaning they cross at a point that is the midpoint of both. However, the two diagonals do not have to be equal in length. As a parallelogram leans away from a rectangle, the diagonals keep their shared midpoint but stretch by different amounts, so they become unequal. Equal diagonals appear only in the special case where all the angles are 90 degrees, which is a rectangle. So bisecting is guaranteed for every parallelogram, but equal length is not.

topics.publication_chunk: A parallelogram is a quadrilateral whose opposite sides are parallel. In any parallelogram, the opposite angles are equal, and each pair of adjacent angles (two angles sharing a side) adds up to 180 degrees. content.text: A rhombus is a quadrilateral in which all four sides are equal. Because its opposite sides turn out to be parallel, every rhombus is also a parallelogram, so its opposite angles are equal and its adjacent angles add to 180 degrees. This means the four angles follow from any one of them, exactly as in a parallelogram: a value, its supplement, and each repeated once. Its perimeter is four times one side. Equal sides do not by themselves make a square, though. A rhombus can lean, keeping all four sides equal while its angles are not 90 degrees. Only when the angles are also 90 degrees does the rhombus become a square.

content.text: The two diagonals of a rhombus always cross at right angles, bisect each other, and bisect the vertex angles they reach. Because they are perpendicular and bisect each other, they cut the rhombus into four right triangles whose legs are the two half diagonals. So each side of the rhombus is the hypotenuse of one of these right triangles, found from the half diagonals, and the area of the rhombus is half the product of its two diagonals. The perpendicular crossing is true for every rhombus, whether upright or leaning. It becomes a square only when the angles are also 90 degrees, and only then do the two diagonals become equal in length.

Premise: A class is told only that the two diagonals are equal and cut each other in half, and is asked to name the shape before anything is drawn.
overview.concept: The diagonals decide the family. Diagonals that bisect each other give a parallelogram. Add equal lengths and it is a rectangle; add a right angle crossing instead and it is a rhombus; add both and it is a square. Because a square is a rectangle, a condition set can name more than one family at once, so the answer is a set.
overview.purpose: The student identifies a quadrilateral family from its diagonal behaviour alone, and sets the diagonals to produce a stated target family.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Diagonals fill the main panel with the readouts to the right on a wide frame and beneath on a 390 px frame. Every endpoint keeps a 44 px hit target and no two are drawn closer than 60 px. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not reveal the outline while a prediction is still open, and never report a single family name where the conditions allow more than one. A single name would teach that equal diagonals force a square.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. The outline is always the quadrilateral formed by joining the four diagonal endpoints in order, so the diagonals fully determine it. Bisecting makes the two halves of each diagonal equal, which forces the opposite sides to match. Equal lengths then force equal diagonals in the outline, and a right angled crossing forces equal sides. Each condition adds exactly one constraint to the outline, which is why they compose. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.summary: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the diagonal conditions from its own values, shows the question, then reveals the readouts, the outline and the family set together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A condition set names a family, and the family named here contains the square rather than being it. Breaks: Equal diagonals assumed to force a square, ignoring every non square rectangle. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): A failed family test is reported as a named missing condition, not as no answer. Breaks: Diagonals treated as decoration, so a figure whose diagonals fail a condition is thought to have no family at all. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): Diagonal conditions guarantee a whole chain of families, so the honest answer is a set. Breaks: Believing each condition set picks out exactly one shape name. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): The crossing point is defined by both diagonals, so it cannot be moved off either of them. Breaks: Treating the crossing point as a free handle rather than as the meeting the conditions are measured from. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): The outline exists only because the four endpoints are not all on one line. Breaks: Forgetting that the outline is built from the diagonals, so a degenerate crossing is expected to draw something.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with two diagonals that are equal and bisect each other, the outline HIDDEN, and asks what shape this must be. Beat 2 reveals the outline as a rectangle and the three readouts are read back as the reason. Beat 3 adds the right angle lock, the outline becomes a square, and the tool says that the earlier answer was a set and not a single shape. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setDiagonals, toggleRightAngle, revealOutline and say. No drag: the agent sets endpoints by position, never by sweeping.
whatYouLearned: Diagonals that bisect each other give a parallelogram
Equal diagonals add the rectangle condition and a right angled crossing adds the rhombus condition
A condition set can name a set of families, because a square is a rectangle and a rhombus at once
conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on two equal diagonals bisecting each other with the outline hidden and all three condition readouts on, and ask the class to name the family out loud. Commit the class name on the prediction pad. Target the two equal diagonals with the crossing at both midpoints. Never reveal the outline before the prediction is committed, and never name the family at this call. Call 2. Reveal the outline and read the three conditions back one at a time as the reason it had to come out that way. Target the outline on. Read both diagonal lengths and the crossing angle from the tool's own readouts, never from this plan. Call 3. Switch the right angle lock on with the same two diagonals in place, and let the outline change. Target the right angle lock on. Say which families the tool now lists in the family set readout, taking the list from the tool's own state and never from memory.

hunts: BUILD THE FAMILY: set the diagonals so the outline is a rhombus that is not a square, then say which condition you left out.
ONE CONDITION AT A TIME: start from a general crossing and turn on one condition at a time, naming what each buys.
NOT A SQUARE: make equal bisecting diagonals give three different rectangles, none of them square.
MISSING PIECE: aim at a target family, get it wrong on purpose, and read which condition the tool names.

observationsAndConclusions.why: The four diagonal endpoints joined in order are the whole figure, so the diagonals determine the outline completely
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The outline is drawn only after the three condition readouts have been read, and it is exactly what they promised
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The diagonals are a defining condition, not a feature to be read off the shape afterwards

observationsAndConclusions.why: Equal lengths and bisection together force the rectangle conditions and nothing further
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Equal diagonals that bisect each other give many different rectangles and only a few of them are squares
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Equal diagonals never force a square, because every rectangle that is not a square has them too

observationsAndConclusions.why: Each condition adds exactly one constraint to the outline, so the conditions compose instead of replacing each other
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Switching the right angle lock on turns the same crossing into a square
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A condition set can name more than one family, which is why the honest answer is sometimes a set of names

media.description: Two crossing segments stand alone on a plain working ground with no figure drawn around them: the diagonals AC and BD, meeting at O. Tick marks carry the bisection (one tick on each half of AC, two on each half of BD, drawn only where that diagonal really is cut in half), a small square at O carries the right-angled crossing, and both lengths and the crossing angle are printed live along the top of the scene. Three labelled booleans - bisect each other, equal in length, meet at right angles - sit beside the figure, and beneath it the tool prints the whole SET of families the current conditions guarantee rather than a single name, so a square is reported as sitting inside the rectangle set and the rhombus set at once. The outline is never drawn independently: it is the quadrilateral A B C D formed by joining the four endpoints in order, and it appears as a consequence of the conditions rather than as a separate piece of evidence. In Free Play the student drags any endpoint, slides the crossing along a diagonal, locks the crossing at 90 degrees and sets a target family, and the tool answers a failed target by NAMING the condition that is still missing. Two positions are refused with the reason on screen - a crossing that is not on both diagonals, and two diagonals dragged towards one straight line - because neither describes a figure that exists.

Beat 3 adds the right angle lock, the outline becomes a square, and the tool says that the earlier answer was a set and not a single shape. concept.notation: The three diagonal conditions are written as bisect each other, equal in length and meet at right angles. A family answer may be a set of names, not a single name.
concept.statement: The diagonals decide the family. Diagonals that bisect each other give a parallelogram. Add equal lengths and it is a rectangle; add a right angle crossing instead and it is a rhombus; add both and it is a square. Because a square is a rectangle, a condition set can name more than one family at once, so the answer is a set.
prerequisites: the diagonal properties of the special quadrilaterals
misconceptions: Diagonals treated as decoration rather than as a defining condition, so they are read off a shape and never used to make one.
Equal diagonals assumed to force a square, ignoring every non square rectangle.
concept.why_it_is_true: The outline is always the quadrilateral formed by joining the four diagonal endpoints in order, so the diagonals fully determine it. Bisecting makes the two halves of each diagonal equal, which forces the opposite sides to match. Equal lengths then force equal diagonals in the outline, and a right angled crossing forces equal sides. Each condition adds exactly one constraint to the outline, which is why they compose.
worked_numbers: Diagonals of 10 and 10 bisecting each other give a rectangle, and only some of those are squares.
Diagonals of 10 and 6 bisecting at right angles give a rhombus that is not a square.
Diagonals of 8 and 8 bisecting at right angles give a square, which is in both of the earlier sets.

revealOutlineOutcomes.on: the four endpoints are joined in order by a thin stroke, and the family set readout is filled in
revealOutlineOutcomes.off: only the two crossing segments and the three condition readouts are on screen, which is the state a prediction is made in

setTargetFamilyOutcomes.kite: the target is met when one diagonal is bisected by the other and they meet at right angles, which the tool marks as the only target the bisect both condition must be dropped for
setTargetFamilyOutcomes.none: no target is set and the tool simply reports the family set the current conditions allow
setTargetFamilyOutcomes.square: the target needs all three conditions at once, and the tool reports the square as sitting inside both earlier sets
setTargetFamilyOutcomes.rhombus: the target is met when the diagonals bisect each other and the crossing angle readout reaches 90
setTargetFamilyOutcomes.rectangle: the target is met when the diagonals bisect each other and their two length readouts agree
setTargetFamilyOutcomes.parallelogram: the target is met as soon as the crossing point is the midpoint of both diagonals, whatever their lengths

toggleRightAngleOutcomes.on: the crossing is locked at 90 degrees and the crossing angle readout freezes there, so the outline gains four equal sides
toggleRightAngleOutcomes.off: the crossing angle is free again and the outline loses its equal sides unless the endpoints happen to keep them

answer_key.worked: Diagonals that are equal and bisect each other name the rectangle family, which includes the square, so the answer is a set and not one shape.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn diagonals: the three boolean conditions, the family set they imply, and whether a target family has been produced.
answer_key.precision: Every condition is measured from the endpoint coordinates with a tolerance of 0.5 degrees and 0.01 units, stated in the feedback. The ground truth is a set of family names, never a single name.
answer_key.ground_truth: bisect(d1, d2) = the crossing point is the midpoint of both. equal(d1, d2) = the two lengths agree within tolerance. perpendicular(d1, d2) = the crossing angle is 90 within tolerance. familySet(conditions) = every family name consistent with them, so a square condition set returns square inside rectangle and rhombus.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists so the class commits a name with the outline NOT yet drawn. The three booleans are the only evidence on screen, which is the whole point: the diagonals have to become a defining condition rather than a feature read off a finished shape. Ask for the name out loud before moving on, and do not say the word square.

Beat 2 is the payoff and it is a consequence, not a new fact. The four endpoints join in order and a rectangle appears, so read the three conditions back one at a time as the reason it had to come out that way. The same 16 and 16 that were on screen a moment ago are still on screen.

Beat 3 adds ONE condition and the earlier answer is seen to have been a set all along. The crossing locks at 90 degrees, the outline becomes a square, and rectangle stays lit beside it. If rectangle went dark the tool would be teaching that a square is not a rectangle, which is the misconception the beat exists to break.

media.title: Name the Shape Before You Draw It
media.context: This hook opens the topic on naming a quadrilateral from its diagonals or from joined triangles. Students know the main families. The film must not match any clue to any shape and must not reveal the triangle surprise.
media.description: Imagine being handed only two crossing lines, told nothing about the corners, and asked to name the quadrilateral they will make. Three simple clues about those diagonals can name the shape before a single side is drawn.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Name a quadrilateral from properties of its diagonals, or from two joined triangles. Key teaching points: 1) Diagonals that bisect each other give a parallelogram. 2) Adding equal diagonals gives a rectangle. 3) Adding perpendicular diagonals instead gives a rhombus. 4) Both conditions together give a square. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often think the diagonals cannot determine the shape. 2) Students often forget that two identical triangles can be joined in more than one way. Pause points: 0:23, at the end of three simple clues: ask which shape equal diagonals alone would give. 0:23, just before the open question: ask what two identical triangles could make. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what the diagonals of a square do. After viewing, ask how many clues are needed to name a shape.

topics.summary: A quadrilateral can be built from its diagonals or from two joined triangles. The learner names the shape from the diagonal clues, and from the triangle type together with the join, a half turn giving a parallelogram and a reflection giving a kite.

content.text: A pair of diagonals that bisect each other already fixes a parallelogram. Two extra clues then decide which special parallelogram it is. If the diagonals are also equal in length, the shape is a rectangle. If instead they cross at a right angle, the shape is a rhombus. If they are both equal and perpendicular, the shape is a square, which is why extending one diagonal of a square, so the diagonals stop being equal, turns it into a rhombus. When the diagonals are perpendicular, the area of the quadrilateral is half the product of the two diagonals. Reading these clues lets you name the shape before joining the ends, rather than guessing.

content.text: When two identical triangles are glued along a matching edge, that shared edge becomes an inside diagonal and the four outer edges become the sides of a quadrilateral. Which quadrilateral you get depends on how the triangles are joined. A half turn about the midpoint of the shared edge sends equal sides to opposite positions, so opposite sides become parallel and equal, giving a parallelogram. A reflection across the shared edge sends equal sides to adjacent positions, giving two adjacent equal pairs, which is a kite. Two identical equilateral triangles give a rhombus because all four outer sides are equal. So the same pair of triangles can make different quadrilaterals, and the joining edge and method matter as much as the triangles themselves.

Which quadrilateral you get depends on how the triangles are joined. A half turn about the midpoint of the shared edge sends equal sides to opposite positions, so opposite sides become parallel and equal, giving a parallelogram. A reflection across the shared edge sends equal sides to adjacent positions, giving two adjacent equal pairs, which is a kite. Two identical equilateral triangles give a rhombus because all four outer sides are equal. So the same pair of triangles can make different quadrilaterals, and the joining edge and method matter as much as the triangles themselves.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer which quadrilateral a pair of diagonals traces before the ends are joined through observation and reasoning, and determine that reading three clues, whether the diagonals are equal, bisect each other, and cross at a right angle, names the shape. They will explain that equal bisecting diagonals give a rectangle, perpendicular bisecting diagonals give a rhombus, both together give a square, and bisecting alone leaves a general parallelogram.
Examine the worked examples of naming a quadrilateral from its diagonals, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving naming a quadrilateral from its diagonals, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer which quadrilateral two identical triangles build when joined edge to edge through observation and reasoning, and determine that the type of triangle and the way they are joined together decide the result. They will explain that a half turn about the shared edge places equal sides opposite to give a parallelogram, while a reflection across the edge places equal sides adjacent to give a kite, so the joining edge matters as much as the triangles.

media.title: The Kite and the Slanted Table
media.context: This hook opens the topic on kites and trapeziums. Students know the parallelogram family. The film must not explain the fold and must not say why a parallelogram counts as a trapezium.
media.description: A paper kite in the sky has a shape all its own: two short sides on top, two long sides below and a special line down its spine. Nearby sits the trapezium, a shape with just one pair of parallel sides, like a table seen from the side.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Describe the kite and the trapezium and see how they relate to the rest of the family. Key teaching points: 1) A kite has two pairs of equal adjacent sides. 2) One of its diagonals is an axis of symmetry. 3) A trapezium has at least one pair of parallel sides. 4) A parallelogram therefore qualifies as a trapezium. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often require a trapezium to have exactly one parallel pair. 2) Students often confuse a kite with a rhombus. Pause points: 0:23, at the end of a table seen from the side: ask which line of the kite is its axis. 0:23, just before the open question: ask whether a parallelogram has a parallel pair. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what makes a kite fold neatly. After viewing, ask how many parallel pairs a trapezium needs.

content.text: A kite is a quadrilateral with two adjacent pairs of equal sides, so its sides read as a pair of one length next to a pair of another length, like 5, 5, 8, 8. Its two diagonals cross at a right angle. One diagonal, called the axis, joins the two vertices where equal sides meet, and it bisects those two vertex angles and is the perpendicular bisector of the other diagonal. The two angles between the unequal sides are equal to each other. Its perimeter is twice the sum of the two side lengths. A kite becomes a rhombus only when both pairs are the same length, making all four sides equal, so most kites are not rhombuses.

content.text: A trapezium is a quadrilateral with at least one pair of parallel sides, called the base and the top. Because a leg crosses these two parallel sides, the two angles it makes with them are co-interior angles, so the two angles on each leg add to 180 degrees. When the two legs are equal in length, the trapezium is an isosceles trapezium, and then the two base angles are equal to each other and the two top angles are equal to each other, each top angle being the supplement of a base angle. Since the rule asks only for at least one parallel pair, a parallelogram, which has two parallel pairs, also counts as a trapezium.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what pattern of sides and diagonals marks a kite through observation and reasoning, and determine that a kite has two adjacent pairs of equal sides, an axis diagonal that bisects the vertex angles it joins and perpendicularly bisects the other diagonal, and equal angles between its unequal sides. They will explain that a kite is a rhombus only when both pairs share one length so that all four sides become equal.

Students will be able to infer what a single pair of parallel sides forces on the angles of a trapezium through observation and reasoning, and determine that the two angles on each leg between the parallel sides add to 180 degrees, and that equal legs make the base angles equal. They will explain that requiring only at least one parallel pair means a parallelogram, which has two such pairs, also counts as a trapezium.

Only the families taught in the chapter may appear.

media.title: Quad Hierarchy Sorter
media.context: CBSE Class 8, Ganita Prakash Ch. 4 Quadrilaterals (old NCERT Ch. 3 Understanding Quadrilaterals). This closes the chapter: every family's defining conditions are already known and the rings are where those conditions are seen to contain one another. NCERT already draws this family diagram - parallelograms holding rectangles and rhombuses, overlapping at squares, with kite and trapezium outside - so the tool is the diagram made testable. The vocabulary is the textbook's: condition, meets every condition, one more condition. The words subset, set, intersection and class inclusion are never used, and 'trapezium' is never written 'trapezoid'.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's placement, the correct regions, and the property that decided it.
whatYouLearned: A family with more conditions sits inside a family with fewer
A square is a rectangle and a rhombus at once, so it sits in five regions
Membership is decided by measured properties, never by the usual name or the orientation

overview.goal: The student places each figure in every region it belongs to, including nested ones, and states what a card must satisfy to move inward.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: Nested rings drawn on a plain ground with a tray of figure cards beneath them, the way sorted cards are laid out inside chalked circles on the floor. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class refuses to put the square card inside the rectangle ring, and the card's own measured properties are asked to settle where it goes.
overview.concept: The families nest because each inner one satisfies every condition of the ones around it plus at least one more. A square meets the rectangle conditions and the rhombus conditions, so it sits in both and therefore in the parallelogram ring and the quadrilateral ring too. Membership is decided by measured properties, not by the name a figure is usually given.
overview.purpose: The student places each figure in every region it belongs to, including nested ones, and states what a card must satisfy to move inward.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Rings fill the main panel with the tray directly beneath. On a 390 px frame the rings shrink to keep every label and the overlap legible and the tray scrolls horizontally. Every card keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not pre-place any card while a prediction is still open, and never let the square rest outside the overlap. A square filed as its own separate shape is the misconception drawn.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Membership is a set of conditions, and adding conditions can only shrink the set of figures that satisfy them. So the family with more conditions sits inside the family with fewer. A square has every rectangle condition, so it cannot fail to be in the rectangle ring, whatever it is usually called. The rings are a picture of that containment and not a filing system for names. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.summary: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the card set from its own figures, shows the question, then reveals the correct regions, the measured properties and the answer together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A figure belongs to every region whose conditions it meets, and the overlap is the only honest place for the square. Breaks: Class inclusion refused, so a square is not counted as a rectangle. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): Regions are decided by measures, so orientation never moves a card. Breaks: Naming by appearance, so a figure in an unusual orientation is placed in the wrong region. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): A card sits in every region whose conditions it meets, so stopping at an outer one leaves the answer unfinished. Breaks: Treating the outermost true region as the card's answer, so inner membership is left out. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): A refusal is checkable when it names the failed condition and the measurement behind it. Breaks: Reading a rejected placement as an opinion of the tool rather than as a failed measurement. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): Nesting is a consequence of adding conditions, not a filing convention for names. Breaks: Reading the diagram as a filing system for shape names rather than as containment of condition sets.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the nested rings EMPTY and asks where a square belongs on the diagram. Beat 2 sorts the obvious cards, each landing in its outermost failing region so the nesting becomes visible. Beat 3 places the square in the overlap of rectangles and rhombuses and refuses every other position, so inclusion is enforced rather than argued. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with placeCard, showProperties, rotateCard and say. No drag: the agent places a card by naming its region.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the empty nested rings with every card face up in the tray, and ask the class to say out loud where the square card belongs. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Target the empty rings and the full tray. Never place a card before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Place the straightforward cards one at a time into their innermost regions and let the rings fill from the outside in, opening each card as it lands so the class hears the properties that decided it. Targets the parallelogram card, the rectangle card and the rhombus card. Read the region counts from the tool's own readout, never from this plan. Call 3. Take the square card and try it in each outer region in turn, letting the tool refuse every placement except the innermost overlap and name the ring it would have to leave each time. Target the square card into the overlap of the rectangle and rhombus rings. Say how many regions the square finally lights, reading the number from the tool's own state.

hunts: DEEPEST CARD: find the card that reaches the innermost region and say which conditions carried it there.
SPIN TEST: rotate three cards through odd angles and check that not one of them changes region.
BUILD TO ORDER: construct a figure that lands in exactly three regions.
BOUNCE HUNT: get each card bounced once on purpose and collect the property named each time.

textbook: Drawing the nested picture of parallelograms, kites, rhombuses, rectangles and squares
Naming the quadrilateral that is both a kite and a parallelogram
Asking whether there can be a quadrilateral that is both a kite and a rectangle
Asking whether every kite is a rhombus, and stating the correct relationship between them
Deciding whether four equal sides and one right angle force a square
Judging whether equal diagonals that bisect each other force a square

observationsAndConclusions.why: A square meets both the rectangle conditions and the rhombus conditions, so it has to lie inside both rings at once
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The square card is refused by every region except the innermost overlap
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A figure sits in every region whose conditions it satisfies, and never only in the one it is named after

observationsAndConclusions.why: Every membership test reads the measured sides, angles and diagonals, and turning a figure changes none of them
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A card turned to an odd angle lands in exactly the same regions it did before
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Naming by appearance fails exactly where measuring succeeds

observationsAndConclusions.why: A rectangle forces right angles but not four equal sides, so it satisfies the parallelogram conditions and fails the rhombus one
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The rectangle card is refused by the rhombus ring while the parallelogram ring accepts it at once
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Moving inward always costs one more condition, and a card that cannot pay it stays where it is

media.description: Nested rings sit on a plain working ground - Quadrilaterals holding Parallelograms, and inside that two overlapping lobes, Rectangles and Rhombuses, whose lens-shaped overlap is drawn as its own region and labelled Squares. A tray of figure cards waits beneath. Every card is a real quadrilateral held as four vertices, so its sides, angles and diagonals are MEASURED rather than looked up by name, and the rings a card belongs to are derived from those measures alone. Dragging a card onto a ring is a claim of membership: the tool locks it in when the claim is exactly right, accepts it as true but incomplete when the card could go further in, and bounces it back naming the condition it failed and printing the measured value that decided it - 23.1 degrees between the pairs that should have been parallel, or an angle of 72 degrees where 90 was asked for. The square card is therefore refused everywhere except the lens, because resting in the rectangles lobe outside it would record the card as not a rhombus. Tapping a card opens its measured properties grouped by the ring each one decides; turning a card recomputes those properties and moves it not one ring; and the student can build a figure of their own on a snapped 0-20 grid and watch the same conditions decide where it belongs. Region counts stay on screen throughout, so containment is a number the class can read and not only a picture.

mods.learn: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the card set from its own figures, shows the question, then reveals the correct regions, the measured properties and the answer together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
mods.ai_demo: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the nested rings EMPTY and asks where a square belongs on the diagram. Beat 2 sorts the obvious cards, each landing in its outermost failing region so the nesting becomes visible. Beat 3 places the square in the overlap of rectangles and rhombuses and refuses every other position, so inclusion is enforced rather than argued. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with placeCard, showProperties, rotateCard and say. No drag: the agent places a card by naming its region.

scenes.subGoal: Nesting is a consequence of adding conditions, not a filing convention for names.
scenes.onScreen: The scene built from this checkpoint's own numbers, the question set cleanly above it, and nothing else. One worked item: the rings, the card, the question, then the correct regions, the measured properties and the answer together.

scenes.valuesShown: Blackboard lines, in order: A region is the set of figures meeting a list of conditions. | Adding a condition can only remove figures from that set. | So the longer list describes a smaller set of figures. | A smaller set of figures that all meet the shorter list sits inside it. | That is why the rings nest instead of standing side by side. Answer: Because adding a condition can only shrink the set, so the longer list sits inside the shorter one

scenes.animation: Card lock: a correct placement settles over 160 ms and every outer ring it now belongs to pulses in turn, so inclusion is shown as a chain rather than a point.
scenes.interaction: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.
scenes.valuesShown: Every readout stays live, so the invariants keep being computed while the student explores

concept.notation: Nested rings are drawn from the outside in: quadrilaterals, then parallelograms, then rectangles and rhombuses, overlapping at squares. Being in an inner region means being in every ring around it.
concept.statement: The families nest because each inner one satisfies every condition of the ones around it plus at least one more. A square meets the rectangle conditions and the rhombus conditions, so it sits in both and therefore in the parallelogram ring and the quadrilateral ring too. Membership is decided by measured properties, not by the name a figure is usually given.
prerequisites: the defining conditions of each family
misconceptions: Class inclusion refused, so a square is not counted as a rectangle.
Naming by appearance, so a figure in an unusual orientation is placed in the wrong region.
concept.why_it_is_true: Membership is a set of conditions, and adding conditions can only shrink the set of figures that satisfy them. So the family with more conditions sits inside the family with fewer. A square has every rectangle condition, so it cannot fail to be in the rectangle ring, whatever it is usually called. The rings are a picture of that containment and not a filing system for names.
worked_numbers: A square of side 5 belongs to squares, rectangles, rhombuses, parallelograms and quadrilaterals, five regions at once.
A rectangle of 8 by 3 belongs to rectangles, parallelograms and quadrilaterals but not to rhombuses.
A rhombus of side 6 with a 70 degree angle belongs to rhombuses, parallelograms and quadrilaterals but not to rectangles.

extra: Every rickshaw is a vehicle, and not every vehicle is a rickshaw
Every mango is a fruit, so the mango basket sits inside the fruit basket
Every member of the cricket team is also a student of the school
A tile that is a floor tile and also a square tile, and is filed under both
Every one rupee coin is money, and not all money is a coin
A stamp album where the local stamps sit inside the country page
Every teacher in the staff room is also a member of the school
A shop list where wheat sits inside grains and grains sit inside food
Every bus on this route is a bus, and not every bus is on this route
textbook: Drawing the nested picture of parallelograms, kites, rhombuses, rectangles and squares
Naming the quadrilateral that is both a kite and a parallelogram
Asking whether there can be a quadrilateral that is both a kite and a rectangle
Asking whether every kite is a rhombus, and stating the correct relationship between them
Deciding whether four equal sides and one right angle force a square
Judging whether equal diagonals that bisect each other force a square

placement.where: Closes the chapter. Every family's conditions are known, and the rings are where those conditions are seen to contain one another.

revealRegionsOutcomes.square: lights the square overlap, the rectangle ring, the rhombus ring, the parallelogram ring and the quadrilateral ring, five regions at once

showPropertiesOutcomes.kite: opens to two pairs of equal touching sides and diagonals that meet at right angles without both being bisected
showPropertiesOutcomes.square: opens to four equal sides, four right angles and diagonals that are equal, bisect each other and cross at right angles
showPropertiesOutcomes.rhombus: opens to four equal sides, equal opposite angles and diagonals that bisect each other at right angles
showPropertiesOutcomes.rectangle: opens to equal opposite sides, four right angles and equal diagonals that bisect each other
showPropertiesOutcomes.trapezium: opens to exactly one pair of parallel sides and no forced diagonal relation
showPropertiesOutcomes.parallelogram: opens to equal opposite sides, equal opposite angles and diagonals that bisect each other

answer_key.worked: A square belongs in the overlap of rectangles and rhombuses, and therefore also in parallelograms and quadrilaterals. Inner membership implies every outer one.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the measured figure: the full set of regions each card belongs to, evaluated from its properties rather than from its name.
answer_key.precision: Membership is a set of boolean predicates evaluated on the figure's measures, so an unusual orientation is handled automatically. Equality uses a tolerance of 0.5 degrees and 0.01 units, stated in the feedback.
answer_key.ground_truth: properties(vertices) = the measured side, angle and diagonal predicates. regions(properties) = every ring whose conditions all hold. A correct placement is the innermost region, and membership of every outer ring follows from it.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.case: The square card
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: It rests only in the overlap of rectangles and rhombuses and every other placement is refused. The refusal names the region the square would have to leave, which is the inclusion argument in one move.

edge_cases.case: A card in an unusual orientation
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Placed by its measured properties, so a tilted rectangle lands exactly where an upright one does. Orientation never changes membership.

edge_cases.case: A card dropped in an outer region when it belongs further in
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Accepted as true but incomplete, and the tool asks whether it could go further in, rather than marking it wrong.

edge_cases.case: A card dropped in a region it fails
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Bounced back with the failed property named and measured, so the reason is the figure and not the label.

edge_cases.case: A figure the student constructs
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Its properties are measured on submission and its regions are derived, so a self built figure is judged by the same predicates as every supplied card.

startingCards.description: The figures the tray opens with, chosen so every region including the overlap has at least one member.

showProperties.description: Print each card's measured properties on its face. Off by default so the sort is a judgement rather than a reading.

constraints: Membership is modelled as a set of boolean predicates evaluated on the figure's measures, then region fit is derived, so unusual orientations are handled without special cases.
Region containment is enforced: a placement in an inner region also counts as membership of every outer region, and the tool never records one without the others.
The square card only rests in the overlap and every other placement is refused with the region it would have to leave named.
The predicate set is shared with the definition checker and the claim judge, so the three tools cannot disagree about the same figure.
Equality checks use a tolerance of 0.5 degrees and 0.01 units, stated in the feedback whenever it decides a placement.

extra.concept_only: Concept carries no questions of its own. Its beats reveal the idea and then run one reasoning beat each, and every number the agent says is read from state.truth.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example rotating a card a child says is a different shape and showing that its regions did not move.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

media.title: The Quadrilateral Family, Sorted
media.context: This is the chapter summary and it plays after the final topic. Every claim it makes has already been taught and practised, so nothing new appears and no fresh figure is analysed. Its job is to trace every property back to congruent triangles.
media.description: You have met rectangles, squares, parallelograms, rhombuses, kites and trapeziums, and they turn out to be one connected family rather than a collection of strangers. Every quadrilateral has four sides, four angles and two diagonals, with its angles totalling two straight angles because one diagonal splits it into two triangles. From there, each family member is sorted by what its properties force: parallelograms have matching opposite sides and angles, rhombuses add equal sides and perpendicular diagonals, rectangles add right angles and equal diagonals, and a square belongs to both branches at once. Kites and trapeziums sit on their own branches, yet the whole family ultimately traces back to triangles.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Restate the properties of each quadrilateral family and trace them back to congruent triangles. Key teaching points: 1) A quadrilateral's angles total three hundred and sixty degrees. 2) A parallelogram has equal opposite sides and angles and bisecting diagonals. 3) A rhombus adds equal sides and perpendicular diagonals. 4) A rectangle adds right angles and equal diagonals. 5) Every property follows from congruent triangles. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often memorise the properties without the triangle arguments. 2) Students often keep the families separate rather than nested. Pause points: 0:30, at the end of the parallelogram: ask which property forces which. 1:14, just before sorted by what is forced: ask where the congruent triangles are hiding. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what a parallelogram's diagonals do. After viewing, ask why a square belongs to two branches.
media.generation_prompt:
INTENT

Close the chapter by showing that the familiar quadrilaterals form a connected family, beginning with the properties shared by every quadrilateral and then sorting each shape by what its defining properties force. Trace the major properties back to triangles, while making the family structure clear through progressive transformations.

STORY

Rectangles, squares, parallelograms, rhombuses, kites and trapeziums are introduced as one connected family rather than isolated shapes. Begin with the common structure of every quadrilateral: four sides, four angles and two diagonals. Show that one diagonal divides the quadrilateral into two triangles, explaining why the angle sum is two straight angles.

Then build the family progressively. A parallelogram has opposite sides parallel, which forces opposite sides and opposite angles to match and makes the diagonals bisect one another. A rhombus adds equal sides and perpendicular diagonals. A rectangle adds right angles and equal diagonals. A square is both a rectangle and a rhombus at the same time. Kites and trapeziums remain on their own branches.

The final idea is that the family is sorted by properties that are forced, not merely by how a figure happens to look. The claims throughout the chapter ultimately trace back to congruent triangles.

MATHEMATICAL TRUTH MODEL

Every value below is the only value that may appear on screen.

EVERY QUADRILATERAL

Every quadrilateral has:
four sides,
four angles,
two diagonals.

Its angle sum is two straight angles, that is 360 degrees.

WHY THE ANGLE SUM WORKS

One diagonal splits the quadrilateral into two triangles.

PARALLELOGRAM

Opposite sides are parallel.
Opposite sides and opposite angles match.
The diagonals cut each other in half.

RHOMBUS

Adds equal sides.
Its diagonals meet at right angles.

RECTANGLE

Adds right angles.
Its diagonals are equal.

SQUARE

A square is both a rectangle and a rhombus at the same time.

KITES AND TRAPEZIUMS

Kites and trapeziums sit on their own branches.

FINAL CONNECTION

Every claim traces back to congruent triangles.
The family sorts itself by what is forced rather than by what is merely drawn.

ANIMATION RULES

Prefer animation over narration wherever a concept can be shown.
Every scene contains at least one transformation that carries meaning.
No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
Reveal progressively; never dump a finished diagram in one Create.
On-screen text minimal; no paragraph of prose on screen at any time.
Objects that persist across scenes are transformed, never recreated.
No decorative-only animation.

The family structure should emerge progressively rather than appearing as a completed family tree immediately.

The general quadrilateral should visibly split into two triangles with one diagonal.
The parallelogram should visibly establish its forced properties.
The rhombus should visibly add equal sides and perpendicular diagonals.
The rectangle should visibly add right angles and equal diagonals.
The square should visibly combine the rectangle and rhombus branches.
Kites and trapeziums should remain distinct branches.

MATHEMATICAL ACCURACY, HIGHEST PRIORITY

100 percent accurate to NCERT Ganita Prakash for Class 8.
Correct notation, terminology, symbols and labels as used in the Class 8 textbook.
Proportions true wherever proportion carries meaning.
If a figure is not to scale it must say so on screen.
No transformation may pass through a mathematically false intermediate state.

LANGUAGE

British spelling.
No em dash and no en dash anywhere, in narration or on screen.
Readable aloud by a student of this grade.
Indian names and places for any person or setting.

NEGATIVE CONSTRAINTS

No value, label or claim absent from the truth model.
No new content: every idea shown has already been taught in the chapter.
No new worked example and no extension beyond the chapter.
No text outside the safe margin.
No overlapping labels.
No external assets, watermarks or branding.
No particles, sparkles or glow.

SELF-CHECK BEFORE OUTPUT

1. Scene durations sum to exactly 90 seconds across 6 scenes.
2. Every number, count and label on screen appears in the truth model and nowhere else.
3. Every mobject named in a beat is declared in the inventory before it is used.
4. Every persisting mobject is transformed into its next form, never recreated.
5. No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
6. All geometry lies within x in [-6.8, 6.8] and y in [-3.8, 3.8]; nothing is cropped.
7. No label overlaps another label; buff at least 0.2 everywhere.
8. British spelling throughout, and no em dash or en dash in narration or on screen.
9. Every idea shown has already been taught inside the chapter; nothing is new.
10. The square is clearly shown as both a rectangle and a rhombus.
11. The angle sum is connected visually to the two triangles created by a diagonal.
12. The family is sorted by forced properties rather than appearance.
13. The final conclusion traces the properties back to congruent triangles.
14. No fresh worked example appears.
