overview.goal: The student asks yes or no questions using correct property vocabulary to identify a hidden quadrilateral, and judges which question splits the board best.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A board of quadrilateral outlines drawn in mixed orientations on a plain ground, with a question list running down beside it. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class describes the secret shape as the diamond looking one, the board cannot answer, and property words become the only currency left.
overview.concept: A figure is identified by its properties, not by what it looks like. Each property question splits the board into the figures that have the property and those that do not, and the answer removes one part. A question that splits the board roughly in half removes the most figures whichever answer comes back, which is why precision and efficiency go together.
overview.purpose: The student asks yes or no questions using correct property vocabulary to identify a hidden quadrilateral, and judges which question splits the board best.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Board fills the main panel, question list to the right on a wide frame and in a scrolling strip beneath on a 390 px frame. Every figure and every question row keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not reveal the secret figure until a guess is made, and never answer a vague question with a yes or a no. Answering it would teach that loose language works.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Every figure on the board has a fixed property vector, so a property question is a filter on that vector and its answer is determined before it is asked. A question whose yes set and no set are very uneven removes only a few figures on the likely answer; an even split removes about half whichever way it goes. Vague wording has no vector to filter against, which is why the board cannot answer it at all. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A question the board can answer has to name a property that every figure has been measured for. Breaks: Informal shape language substituting for properties, so a figure is described as looking like a diamond. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): A question buys nothing when every live figure gives the same answer. Breaks: Judging a question by whether it is about a real property rather than by whether the live figures disagree about it. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): A question is judged by the worse of its two outcomes, so an even split is worth most. Breaks: Judging a question by how good the lucky answer would be rather than by the worse outcome. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): Identical property vectors cannot be separated by property questions, however many are asked. Breaks: Believing there is always another question that would narrow the board further. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): Property vectors are orientation free, so recognition by appearance is never needed. Breaks: Naming by appearance rather than by definition, so an unusual orientation defeats recognition.

Beat 2 asks a property question and the board greys out, with the split reported as a pair of counts. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with chooseSecret, askQuestion, showSplit and say.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the full board with a secret figure chosen, nothing greyed and no question asked, and ask the class which single question would remove the most shapes. Commit the class question on the prediction pad. Target the full board with no question asked. Never ask a question before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Ask the property question the class chose, let the eliminated figures grey out in place, and read the split back as a pair of counts. Target one property question from the list. Read both counts and the number of figures still live from the tool's own readouts, never from this plan. Call 3. Ask a vague question about what the figure looks like and let the board refuse it, then put the same intention into property words and ask it again. Target one vague question followed by one property question. Say how many figures each of the two removed, taking both numbers from the tool's own state.

observationsAndConclusions.why: The board splits into the figures with the property and the figures without it, and an even split removes about half either way
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A question about the diagonals greys out close to half the board whichever answer comes back
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A good question is one whose two answers are both worth asking about

observationsAndConclusions.why: Only a small part of the board satisfies so strong a property, so the no branch leaves nearly everything standing
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Asking whether the figure is a square removes very little when the answer comes back no
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A very uneven split buys almost nothing on its likely answer

observationsAndConclusions.why: A vague description names no property, so the board has nothing to test each figure against
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A question about what the figure looks like returns a prompt to be more precise and eliminates nothing
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Precise property language is not politeness, it is the only thing the board can act on

media.description: Sixteen quadrilaterals stand on a plain board as outlines in mixed orientations, each wearing the marks the chapter actually uses — tick hatches for equal sides, a small square in a right-angled corner, matching arrowheads on parallel sides and its two diagonals drawn dashed — and no figure carries its family name, because reading the name off the picture is the habit this tool exists to break. One figure is secret. A question is a property statement the board answers from that figure's own record: the figures that disagree with the answer desaturate in one 240 ms wave but stay exactly where they are, so the shape of the board is preserved and the size of the cut is seen rather than counted, and the split the question achieved is printed beside it as a pair of counts. A vague question — does it look like a diamond — is offered on purpose as a decoy and is refused with a prompt to name a property; it removes nothing at all while the question counter still ticks, which is the whole argument for the vocabulary. Because the records are read from measured sides, angles and diagonals, a figure turned by a third of a turn is eliminated by exactly the same questions as an upright one, and two figures that share a record are declared inseparable rather than being questioned forever. A guess is checked against the secret figure and reported together with how many figures were still live when it was made, so a deduction and a gamble are told apart.

mods.ai_demo: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the full board and a secret figure chosen, and asks which single question would remove the most shapes. concept.notation: A question is a property statement answered yes or no, for example do the diagonals bisect each other. A vague description is not a question the board can answer.
concept.statement: A figure is identified by its properties, not by what it looks like. Each property question splits the board into the figures that have the property and those that do not, and the answer removes one part. A question that splits the board roughly in half removes the most figures whichever answer comes back, which is why precision and efficiency go together.
prerequisites: the property vocabulary for sides, angles and diagonals
the quadrilateral families and what defines each
misconceptions: Informal shape language substituting for properties, so a figure is described as looking like a diamond.
Naming by appearance rather than by definition, so an unusual orientation defeats recognition.
concept.why_it_is_true: Every figure on the board has a fixed property vector, so a property question is a filter on that vector and its answer is determined before it is asked. A question whose yes set and no set are very uneven removes only a few figures on the likely answer; an even split removes about half whichever way it goes. Vague wording has no vector to filter against, which is why the board cannot answer it at all.
worked_numbers: Do the diagonals bisect each other splits a sixteen figure board close to eight and eight.
Is it a square splits it about one and fifteen, so it removes very little on a no.
Does it look like a diamond has no property vector and returns a prompt to be more precise.

makeGuessOutcomes.kite: wins only if the secret figure has two pairs of equal touching sides and is not a rhombus
makeGuessOutcomes.square: wins only if the secret figure measures as a square, and a guess made while several figures are still live is recorded as a gamble
makeGuessOutcomes.rhombus: wins only if the secret figure has four equal sides and no right angle
makeGuessOutcomes.rectangle: wins only if the secret figure has four right angles and its adjacent sides are unequal
makeGuessOutcomes.trapezium: wins only if the secret figure has exactly one pair of parallel sides
makeGuessOutcomes.parallelogram: wins only if the secret figure has equal opposite sides and fails both the rectangle and the rhombus conditions

showSplitOutcomes.on: each asked question prints the pair of counts it produced, so the questions can be compared against each other
showSplitOutcomes.off: the figures still grey out but the counts are hidden, so the quality of a question has to be judged by eye

askQuestionOutcomes.isItASquare: splits the board very unevenly, so a no removes very little and the question is a poor one to open with
askQuestionOutcomes.allSidesEqual: keeps only the rhombuses and squares on the yes side, so a no leaves most of the board standing
askQuestionOutcomes.allAnglesRight: keeps only the rectangles and squares on the yes side
askQuestionOutcomes.diagonalsAreEqual: splits the board unevenly, keeping the rectangles and squares on the yes side
askQuestionOutcomes.oppositeSidesEqual: keeps every parallelogram family on the yes side and removes the kites and trapeziums on a no
askQuestionOutcomes.doesItLookLikeADiamond: eliminates nothing and returns a prompt to name a property instead, because the board has no such field to test
askQuestionOutcomes.diagonalsBisectEachOther: splits the board close to half and half, because it separates the parallelogram families from the rest
askQuestionOutcomes.diagonalsMeetAtRightAngles: splits the board unevenly, keeping the rhombuses, squares and kites on the yes side
askQuestionOutcomes.twoPairsOfAdjacentSidesEqual: keeps the kites, rhombuses and squares on the yes side
askQuestionOutcomes.exactlyOnePairOfParallelSides: keeps only the trapeziums that are not parallelograms, so a yes ends the game almost at once

answer_key.worked: A good question splits the board roughly in half. Do the diagonals bisect each other does; is it a square does not.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the board's property vectors: which figures each answer eliminates, the split each question achieved, and whether the final guess is the secret figure.
answer_key.precision: A property vector is precomputed per figure at load, and questions are evaluated as vector filters, so elimination is instant and the split statistic is free.
answer_key.ground_truth: propertyVector(figure) = the fixed boolean vector of its properties. eliminate(question, answer) = the figures whose vector disagrees. split(question) = the pair of counts, computed before the question is answered. isInformative(question) = both counts greater than zero.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.case: A vague question such as does it look like a diamond
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Returns a prompt to be more precise rather than an answer. It is offered as a decoy on purpose, so the refusal is the lesson and not an oversight.

edge_cases.case: A question that eliminates nothing
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Flagged as uninformative with its split reported as all to none, so the student sees why it was wasted rather than only that it failed.

edge_cases.case: A figure in an unusual orientation
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Its property vector is computed from measures, so rotation never changes which questions eliminate it. Naming by appearance fails here by construction.

edge_cases.case: Two figures with identical property vectors
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The tool says no further question can separate them and offers a guess between the two, rather than letting the student ask forever.

edge_cases.case: A guess made early
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Allowed, and the tool reports how many figures were still live when it was made, so a lucky guess is visibly different from a deduction.

constraints: A property vector is precomputed per figure at load and every question is evaluated as a vector filter, which makes elimination instant and the split statistic free.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example asking a question a child proposes and reporting the split it actually achieved.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

tool_config.tool_objective: The student asks yes or no questions using correct property vocabulary to identify a hidden quadrilateral, and judges which question splits the board best.

steps: Every figure on the board carries a vector of measured properties.
A question is answered by filtering that vector.
Looks like a diamond names no measured property, so there is nothing to filter on.
Answering it either way would report a result no measurement supports.
So the board removes 0 figures and asks for a property instead.
items.answer: Because it names no measured property, so there is nothing on the vectors to filter
items.method: Explain why a vague question receives no yes or no
items.question: A student asks whether the hidden figure looks like a diamond. Why does the board answer with a prompt instead of yes or no?

stickers.type_method: Explain why a vague question receives no yes or no

items.checkpoint: A question the board can answer has to name a property that every figure has been measured for.
items.misconception: Informal shape language substituting for properties, so a figure is described as looking like a diamond.

steps: Every figure whose diagonals bisect each other also has equal opposite sides.
So all 10 live figures answer yes.
The split is 10 to nothing, whichever way it was going to go.
A question only removes figures when the live set disagrees about it.
items.answer: Because every live figure answers the same way, so the split is 10 to nothing
items.method: Diagnose a question that eliminates nothing
items.question: Only the 10 figures with bisecting diagonals are still live. The student asks whether the opposite sides are equal and nothing greys out. Why was the question wasted?

stickers.type_method: Diagnose a question that eliminates nothing

items.checkpoint: A question buys nothing when every live figure gives the same answer.
items.misconception: Judging a question by whether it is about a real property rather than by whether the live figures disagree about it.

steps: A question splits the board into the figures that answer yes and those that answer no.
The answer removes one of the two parts, and you do not choose which.
So a question is worth what it leaves in the worse case.
The square question leaves 14 live if the answer is no.
The other question leaves at most 9.
The more even split is the better question.
items.answer: Are two pairs of adjacent sides equal, because its worst case leaves 9 rather than 14
items.method: Compare two questions by the worst case they leave
items.question: Two opening questions are offered on the full board of 16: is it a square, and are two pairs of adjacent sides equal. Which is the better one, and why?

stickers.type_method: Compare two questions by the worst case they leave

items.checkpoint: A question is judged by the worse of its two outcomes, so an even split is worth most.
items.misconception: Judging a question by how good the lucky answer would be rather than by the worse outcome.

steps: Each figure is identified by its vector of measured properties.
These two carry the same vector.
Any question filters on the vector, so it keeps both or removes both.
No further question can separate them, so the tool says so and offers a guess between the two.
items.answer: It declares them inseparable and offers a guess, because identical vectors cannot be split by any property question
items.method: Recognise two figures no property question can separate
items.question: Two figures are still live and every remaining question gives the same answer for both. What does the tool do, and why is that not a failure of the questions?

stickers.type_method: Recognise two figures no property question can separate

items.checkpoint: Identical property vectors cannot be separated by property questions, however many are asked.
items.misconception: Believing there is always another question that would narrow the board further.

steps: Every property vector is computed from measured sides, angles and diagonals.
Turning a figure changes none of those measures.
So its vector is exactly what it was before.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 is the notation, not a warm-up. The class has to see that every figure has been MEASURED — the ticks, the corner squares, the arrowheads and the dashed diagonals are what every later question filters on — because a child who thinks the board is just pictures will keep answering from the pose.

Beat 2 is the argument in one motion: one question, six figures desaturate in place, and the split prints 10 | 6. Read both counts aloud from the tool. The number that matters is not how many went, it is that the board decided it before the question was asked.

Beat 3 is the refusal, and it must be allowed to cost something. The vague question changes nothing on the board while the asked counter still goes up: imprecision is not rude, it is unanswerable. Then put the same intention into property words and ask it again.

media.title: Chapter Summary, The Quadrilateral Hierarchy
media.context: Plays on M6.S8.T8.C85, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: A 165-second whiteboard-style overview that builds the quadrilateral family Venn diagram one oval at a time on a pure white canvas. Trapezium is drawn first as the large outer oval in Navy Blue, then Parallelogram nests inside it, then Rectangle and Rhombus appear as two overlapping Orange ovals whose overlap lights up and is labelled Square in Dark Green; finally a separate Kite oval slides in to overlap the Rhombus region. As each shape's name appears, a small property card pops up beside it listing its sides, angles, and diagonals, with the 90 degrees angle marks, equal-side tick marks, and bisecting-diagonal arrows colour-coded. On-screen captions read "Step 1", "Step 2", "Step 3", and a closing banner shows "angle-sum = 360 degrees" above every shape.
media.teaching_notes: Play this video at the very end of the chapter, during review, once every individual quadrilateral and its diagonal facts have already been taught, it pulls all six shapes into a single picture. Pause around 1:32, right after the narrator asks "where should Rectangle and Rhombus go?" and before the overlap is revealed, and have learners sketch their own guess on paper. Pause again around 2:12 when the Square region flashes. As an attempt-before-reveal prompt, ask at the first pause: "Predict the next step, should Rectangle sit inside, outside, or overlapping Rhombus, and where does Square end up?" At the second pause ask "Why did we do that, why does a square also belong to five other families?" so learners reason from the definitions rather than memorising the diagram.
media.generation_prompt: Duration: 165 seconds. Style: 2D animation, clean whiteboard-style, step-by-step reveal. Background pure white. Font: Lilly. Scene sequence (3 to 5 scenes, each with an explicit time range and a quoted narrator line): Scene 1 (0:00-0:30), states the idea. Six small quadrilaterals are sketched in a row in grey: rectangle, square, parallelogram, rhombus, kite, trapezium, each labelled. Narrator: "Six shapes, one family. Notice how every one of these is still just a quadrilateral, so let's see how they nest together." A banner appears reading "angle-sum = 360 degrees". Scene 2 (0:30-1:05), sets up what is given. The property cards build in Navy Blue for structure: a rectangle card shows all four angles marked 90 degrees with opposite sides ticked equal and diagonals drawn equal and bisecting; a parallelogram card shows opposite sides parallel with arrows, adjacent angles summing to 180 degrees, diagonals bisecting. Narrator: "The key insight here is that each shape adds one rule to a more general one, a rectangle is a parallelogram with all angles ninety degrees." Scene 3 (1:05-1:35), reveals one step at a time. The Venn diagram begins: Navy Blue outer oval labelled Trapezium, then a Parallelogram oval nests inside in Navy Blue, with a pale yellow soft highlight sweeping the nested region. Narrator: "Because a trapezium needs at least one pair of parallel sides, every parallelogram sits inside it. Pause here, what would you do next: where should Rectangle and Rhombus go?" Hold a 3-second pause before revealing. Scene 4 (1:35-2:10), reveals the overlap. Two Orange ovals, Rectangle and Rhombus, appear overlapping inside Parallelogram; their overlap region lights up and is labelled Square in Dark Green with tick marks for equal sides and 90 degrees angle marks. A separate Orange Kite oval slides in to overlap the Rhombus region. Narrator: "Rectangle adds equal angles, Rhombus adds equal sides, and where they overlap you get a Square, equal sides and right angles." Scene 5 (2:10-2:45), checks and recaps. The full diagram is shown; the Square region flashes and a list of five names pops up beside it in Dark Green: rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram, kite, trapezium. The "angle-sum = 360 degrees" banner re-appears across the top. Narrator: "So a square also belongs to five other families, rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram, kite, and trapezium, and every shape here obeys the same three-hundred-and-sixty-degree angle-sum. That's the whole family in one picture." Narration style: calm, instructional, using phrases like "Notice how..." and "The key insight here is...". Music: none, or very subtle. Visual elements: the 5-colour palette, Navy Blue for structure and invariant set boundaries (Trapezium, Parallelogram), Orange for the parts being added or highlighted (Rectangle, Rhombus, Kite ovals), pale yellow for soft highlight sweeps, grey for the secondary row of sample shapes, white canvas; arrows showing the nesting transformations. Givens and definitions in Navy Blue, each added constraint in Orange, and the final Square label and membership list in Dark Green. M0 accuracy: every 90 degrees angle mark drawn at ninety degrees within one degree, equal sides drawn equal with matching tick marks, perpendicular diagonals of the rhombus and square crossing at a true right angle, and the Venn nesting drawn exactly as narrated, Parallelogram fully inside Trapezium, Square exactly at the Rectangle-Rhombus overlap, Kite overlapping only the Rhombus region; the spoken count of five other families must match the five names shown in the list.

content.text: All the special quadrilaterals fit into one nested family. A parallelogram has parallel opposite sides; the rectangle and the rhombus are both special parallelograms, and the square, having all the properties of both, sits in the overlap of rectangle and rhombus. Because at least one parallel pair is enough for a trapezium, the parallelogram lies inside the trapezium family too. The kite reaches outside the parallelogram, meeting it only at the rhombus. The key idea is that membership follows from which properties hold, so a single clue, like equal and bisecting diagonals, only rules shapes out; it names a rectangle but not necessarily a square, and perpendicular diagonals name neither a rhombus nor a kite on their own. This is why a square is at once a rectangle, a rhombus, and a parallelogram.

content.text: A quadrilateral is identified by the properties it has, not by what it resembles. Asking whether the diagonals bisect each other, or whether the opposite sides are equal, narrows a set of candidates because every figure either has that property or does not. A question that splits the candidates roughly in half removes the most figures whichever answer comes back. Loose descriptions such as it looks like a diamond narrow nothing, because there is no property to test them against.

objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what separates a quadrilateral from other outlines through observation and reasoning, and determine that a figure qualifies exactly when it is closed, is built from four straight sides, and has sides that meet only at their endpoints. They will explain that a curved side, an open gap, a crossing, or the wrong number of sides rules a figure out, while a figure that passes shows four vertices, four angles, and two diagonals.
Examine the worked examples of what makes a figure a quadrilateral, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving what makes a figure a quadrilateral, across different cases.

Students will be able to state both definitions of a rectangle, one by all four angles being 90 degrees and one by the diagonals being equal and bisecting each other, and state that a square is a rectangle with all four sides equal. They will test a given quadrilateral against either definition and explain why the two definitions agree.

Students will be able to infer what two crossing strips must satisfy to trace a rectangle through observation and reasoning, and determine that four endpoints form a rectangle exactly when the diagonals are equal in length and cross at their shared midpoints, whatever angle they cross at. They will explain that unequal diagonals lean the figure into a parallelogram and off centre crossings fail, so a rectangle's own diagonals are always equal and bisect each other.

Students will be able to infer what the crossing angle of the equal diagonals fixes at each corner through observation and reasoning, and determine that a crossing angle x splits a right angle corner into a half of 180 minus x and a half of x, which always add to 90 degrees. They will explain that all four corner triangles are isosceles because the half diagonals are equal, and that when x is 90 both corner parts become 45, the special square case.

Students will be able to infer what one extra condition turns a rectangle into a square through observation and reasoning, and determine that equal diagonals which bisect each other and also cross at a right angle force all four sides equal. They will explain that the perpendicular crossing is the single extra demand beyond a rectangle, that a square's diagonals are equal, bisect each other and meet at 90 degrees, and that each diagonal cuts a corner into two 45 degree halves.
Examine the worked examples of the square as a special rectangle, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving the square as a special rectangle, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: The Angle Sum of a Quadrilateral
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what the four angles of any quadrilateral add to, however its corners are dragged, through observation and reasoning, and determine that the total is always 360 degrees, so a missing angle is 360 minus the other three. They will explain that one diagonal splits the figure into two triangles of 180 degrees each, and that three right angles use up 270 degrees so the fourth angle is forced to be 90.

Students will be able to infer how the four angles of a parallelogram depend on any single one through observation and reasoning, and determine that opposite angles are equal while each pair of adjacent angles adds to 180 degrees, so the angles read as a value, its supplement, the value, and the supplement around the figure. They will explain that a side acts as a transversal across the parallel sides, making adjacent angles co-interior and so supplementary, which forces the opposite angles to match.
Examine the worked examples of angles of a parallelogram, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving angles of a parallelogram, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer what a parallelogram's diagonals must share and what they need not share through observation and reasoning, and determine that the opposite sides are equal and the two diagonals bisect each other, yet the diagonals need not be equal in length. They will explain that congruent triangles force a shared midpoint while nothing forces matching lengths, so equal diagonals belong to the rectangle rather than to every parallelogram.

Students will be able to infer how the angles of a four equal sided figure behave through observation and reasoning, and determine that a rhombus is a parallelogram, so its opposite angles are equal and its adjacent angles add to 180 degrees, letting all four angles follow from any one. They will explain that equal sides alone do not make a square, since a leaning rhombus keeps its four equal sides while its angles move away from 90 degrees.

Students will be able to infer how the diagonals of a rhombus cross and what they reveal about its sides through observation and reasoning, and determine that the diagonals meet at right angles, bisect each other, and bisect the vertex angles, so each side is the hypotenuse of the right triangle formed by the two half diagonals. They will explain that this perpendicular crossing holds for every rhombus, so it is a square only when its angles are also 90 degrees and its diagonals become equal.

Students will be able to infer which quadrilateral a pair of diagonals traces before the ends are joined through observation and reasoning, and determine that reading three clues, whether the diagonals are equal, bisect each other, and cross at a right angle, names the shape. They will explain that equal bisecting diagonals give a rectangle, perpendicular bisecting diagonals give a rhombus, both together give a square, and bisecting alone leaves a general parallelogram.
Examine the worked examples of naming a quadrilateral from its diagonals, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving naming a quadrilateral from its diagonals, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer which quadrilateral two identical triangles build when joined edge to edge through observation and reasoning, and determine that the type of triangle and the way they are joined together decide the result. They will explain that a half turn about the shared edge places equal sides opposite to give a parallelogram, while a reflection across the edge places equal sides adjacent to give a kite, so the joining edge matters as much as the triangles.

Students will be able to infer what pattern of sides and diagonals marks a kite through observation and reasoning, and determine that a kite has two adjacent pairs of equal sides, an axis diagonal that bisects the vertex angles it joins and perpendicularly bisects the other diagonal, and equal angles between its unequal sides. They will explain that a kite is a rhombus only when both pairs share one length so that all four sides become equal.

Students will be able to infer what a single pair of parallel sides forces on the angles of a trapezium through observation and reasoning, and determine that the two angles on each leg between the parallel sides add to 180 degrees, and that equal legs make the base angles equal. They will explain that requiring only at least one parallel pair means a parallelogram, which has two such pairs, also counts as a trapezium.

Students will be able to infer how the special quadrilaterals nest inside one family through observation and reasoning, and determine that the square sits in the overlap of rectangle and rhombus, both inside the parallelogram, with the kite and trapezium reaching outside. They will explain that every membership follows from which defining properties hold, so a single diagonal clue only rules shapes out, naming a rectangle without pinning down a square.

how_to_use.intro: Each section is one topic, split into small microconcepts. Every microconcept pairs a short, plain explanation with one interactive tool, so a property is discovered by dragging and predicting before it is ever stated.

points.text: Every idea is explored by hand, building or reshaping a quadrilateral, before it is practised.
points.title: One tool per section

points.text: The tool withholds the answer: the student predicts the shape or angle first, then the tool confirms it green or corrects it red.
points.title: Predict then reveal

points.text: Properties are justified by congruent triangles, not by measuring one figure, because measuring cannot prove the next case.
points.title: Deduce, do not measure

points.text: A few sections add a video for motivation, a compass construction, or a recap; it always plays after the tool so it never pre-empts discovery.
points.title: Video after the tool

points.text: After the tool-answered practice, four reasoning items ask the learner to apply, work backwards, explain, and catch a deliberate mistake.
points.title: Think it through

summary_stats.counts_note: One distinct tool per concept; each tool runs four mods (AI demo, Learn, Practice, Free Play), with one objective each for AI demo, Learn and Practice and none for Free Play.
summary_stats.videos_note: One 30 to 40 second curiosity hook video per topic, plus a chapter intro video and a chapter summary video of 1 to 2 minutes each.
summary_stats.tool_needed_note: Per-item boolean for how the ANSWER is entered, NOT whether to show the tool. The frontend ALWAYS renders the tool. true = the answer must be produced through the tool. false = the student reasons it out (typed/spoken) and the tool stays on screen as an aid.
summary_stats.solved_examples_note: Each solved example carries a first-person 'reasoning' field that generalises the method.
summary_stats.practice_problems_note: 201 practice items in all = (14 microconcepts x 10 tool-answered) + (14 x 4 reasoning items) + 5 proof items on the concepts that state a general claim.
summary_stats.question_repository_note: Worked-example and practice questions are no longer inline. Each learn/practice concept carries a question_bank_ref into question_repository.json; the teacher agent pulls questions from the repository at teach time. The teaching (AI-demo) concept keeps its inline source_ai_reasoning block.

authoring_rules.nesting: Each objective contains exactly one concept; each concept contains its solved examples then its practice questions.
authoring_rules.solved_examples: At least 10 per microconcept; each is demonstrated on that section's tool with numbered steps, a final answer and first-person reasoning that models how to think, not just which buttons to press.
authoring_rules.practice_questions: At least 10 tool-answered items per microconcept (marked right/wrong on the tool), followed by exactly 4 reasoning items: application, reverse, explain, error_spotting. A concept that states a general claim carries a 5th reasoning item, proof, between explain and error_spotting.
